newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ruling bloc moves towards loose alliance.
newsitem.headline: Japan ruling bloc moves towards loose alliance.

text.p: The parties in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's outgoing coalition moved on Tuesday to set up a loose, out-of-government alliance instead of renewing their formal coalition arrangement, party officials said.

Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) failed to win a parliamentary majority in Lower House elections on October 20 and has yet to seal a policy agreement with the Social Democrats and the Sakigake party, its old allies.
On Tuesday, the three parties agreed to set up a forum outside the cabinet to discuss policy issues, Social Democratic party officials said.

"The shape of the new alliance is beginning to take shape. It would be out-of-cabinet cooperation," a senior Social Democratic Party official said. "We will set up a three-party forum to discuss policy issues."

The LDP needs the parliamentary seats held by the two other parties to command majorities in both the upper and lower houses. Parliament is almost certain to reconvene on November 7 to elect a new prime minister.

Although Hashimoto is assured of re-election, his government may have to rule with only a minority, propped up by a loose alliance of the three parties, instead of a solid coalition, coalition officials said.
The likely new arrangement would mean the old coalition partners would not have members in the new Hashimoto cabinet, the Social Democrat officials and other coalition officials said.

For a minority government, the possibility of a no-confidence motion in parliament is always present. If such a motion were carried it would lead to early general elections. Polls for the powerful Lower House need not be called until October 2000, but the chamber can be dissolved anytime.

In Tuesday's talks, the three parties agreed to re-endorse the official government position of expressing remorse for Japan's World War Two actions first announced by Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama in August 1995.
They also agreed to set up a parliamentary watchdog group to oversee the conduct of bureaucrats, a move following several scandals involving the finance and health ministries.

But the LDP and Social Democrats remain far apart on the Social Democrat's demands to cut back the number of U.S. troops on Okinawa and scale back proposed security commitments under the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.
Another sticking point is a Social Democrat demand to ban corporations from donating funds to parties, anathema to the pro-business LDP.
The concentration of U.S. troops and military facilities on southern Japan's Okinawa island flared up last year after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by U.S. servicemen.
Okinawa hosts 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan and half of the 44,000 U.S. military personnel in the country.
Last month, Okinawans voted overwhelmingly in a non-binding provincial referendum for a reduction in the U.S. presence.
The three parties may issue a formal joint policy statement on Thursday, including plans to set up the standing forum, party sources said.

The LDP has also been trying to win support from several independents and defectors from the opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), but the prospective number is far below the 12 needed to give the LDP a majority in the Lower House.
